What's Happening in Your Child's Brain
The Neuroscience — Plain English
When your child's brain has something to communicate — pain, fear, need, overwhelm — a signal fires. In a typically developing child, this signal travels to the expressive language centers (Broca's area, left hemisphere), accesses vocabulary, and emerges as words.
In many autistic children, this pathway is differently wired. The expressive language centers may be less accessible, less reliable, or entirely unavailable under stress. The signal doesn't complete the journey to words. But the need to communicate doesn't disappear. It re-routes. It finds the motor system. It finds what works.
The Critical Insight
This is not a behavior problem. This is a communication infrastructure problem. The child has an intact message and no reliable delivery system. Self-injury is not the problem — it's the improvised solution to a problem we created by not providing better tools.
Clinical Term:Communication-Function Self-Injurious Behavior (SIB) / Functionally-Maintained Self-Injury / Expressive Communication Deficit with Behavioral Expression
📖Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): Neurological basis for communication-behavior intersections in ASD. DOI:10.3389/fnint.2020.556660 | FCT core mechanism research: NIH PMC1286182
Where Communication-Based Self-Injury Sits in Your Child's Journey

⚠️You are likely here: Your child is in the 2–12 age window, either non-speaking or minimally verbal, and has discovered that self-injury is their most reliable communication tool. This is the highest-impact window for intervention. Neural plasticity is still high. The habit has not yet calcified. The window is open.

Functional Communication Training (FCT) for Communication-Based Self-Injurious Behavior
"Giving Your Child a Voice That Doesn't Require Pain"

Communication-Based Self-Injury (SIB) occurs when a child engages in self-harm — head-hitting, biting themselves, scratching, hair-pulling, head-banging — because this behavior reliably gets their needs met when nothing else does. The self-injury is communication. It's the child's most effective language. Functional Communication Training (FCT) is the evidence-based intervention that replaces the self-injury by teaching an alternative communication form — a word, a sign, a picture card, a device button — that serves the same function and works equally well. When "I need help" can be pressed on a device as easily as hitting, hitting becomes unnecessary. This technique is not about stopping a behavior. It is about building a language.
🧩 Domain
Challenging Behavior & Functional Communication
📅 Age
2–12 years
⏱ Session
10–20 minutes
🔁 Frequency
Daily — embedded in natural routines
📊 Outcome
6–12 weeks for primary replacement

The Consortium Behind D-410 — Who Uses This Technique
🗣 SLP — Primary Lead
AAC selection, communication system design, FCT language targets, device programming, and partner training. The speech-language pathologist designs the voice your child will use.
🧠 ABA / BCBA — Primary Lead
Functional behavior assessment, FCT protocol design, reinforcement systems, data collection, and generalization planning. Measures and validates every replacement behavior.
✋ OT — Supporting Role
Motor access to communication devices, device mounting and positioning, and fine motor precision for pointing and symbol selection.
📚 SpEd — Supporting Role
Classroom implementation, partner training, school communication systems, and curriculum access via AAC across all educational settings.
🩺 NeuroDev Pediatrics — Medical
Medical rule-out for underlying pain conditions (GI, dental, ENT) that may be driving SIB; medication review where warranted.

9 Materials That Give Your Child a Voice Without Pain

Each material below is mapped to a specific function of Communication-Based SIB. Before purchasing, identify your child's primary SIB function (communication of needs? pain? escape? attention?). Start with the material that addresses that function first.
Core Communication Boards with High-Priority Messages
Survival vocabulary: HELP · STOP · HURT · SCARED · WANT · DON'T WANT · MORE · ALL DONE · BREAK. Always present. Always honored. ₹200–800 or ₹0 DIY.
SGDs (Speech-Generating Devices) and AAC Apps
Devices that speak the child's message aloud. Free apps (LetMeTalk, CBoard) to dedicated SGDs. ₹0–50,000+.
Pain and Body Sensation Communication Tools
Body maps, pain scales, symptom cards. Converts hitting-as-locator into pointing-as-communicator. ₹100–500.
Emotional Expression Visuals and Regulation Tools
Feeling faces cards, Zones of Regulation, body-emotion connection cards, regulation choice boards. ₹200–1,000.
Request and Rejection Communication Systems
"I WANT" sentence strips, YES/NO symbols, PECS-style systems for requesting and refusing. ₹100–800.
Attention / Help-Seeking Alternatives
Call buttons, HELP cards, colored flag systems, vibrating attention-getters. ₹200–1,500.
Escape and Break Request Systems
Break cards, TOO HARD signals, ALL DONE cards, timer-based break systems. ₹100–400.
Visual Schedules and Predictability Supports

Material 1 — Core Communication Boards with High-Priority Messages
What It Is
High-contrast, laminated communication boards carrying your child's most critical messages — not comprehensive vocabulary, but survival vocabulary: HELP · STOP · HURT · SCARED · WANT · DON'T WANT · MORE · ALL DONE · BREAK. Always present. Always honored. The board is their emergency voice.
Why It Works
Every time the child uses the board instead of self-injury, and every time the message is immediately honored, the child's brain learns: communication works. I don't need to hurt myself to be heard. This is the core learning loop of FCT.
Key Insight
Start with the 6–8 messages that replace self-injury specifically. HELP, STOP, HURT, and ALL DONE. Comprehensive vocabulary comes later.
Safety Principle
The board must WORK every time. If the board is present but messages are not honored, the child learns that communication is unreliable — and self-injury remains the superior option.
Product Options
  • Laminated core vocabulary boards (pre-made, A4 or A5 size) — ₹200–800
  • Velcro-attachable wearable mini boards
  • High-contrast symbol cards (printed, laminated)
🔍Search Amazon.in: "Core Vocabulary Communication Board AAC"

DIY ₹0 Version: Print body-sized cards with 6–8 symbols (Boardmaker Free Symbols). Laminate at any stationery shop (₹10–20/sheet). Post identical copies in every room. The paper version works exactly as well as the premium version, if it is always present and always honored.
Material 2 — SGDs (Speech-Generating Devices) and AAC Apps
What It Is
Speech-generating devices (SGDs) speak the child's message aloud. When a child presses "I NEED HELP" and the device says it in clear audio, every communication partner — regardless of whether they know the child's signs or symbols — can hear and respond. AAC apps on tablets (Proloquo2Go, Avaz, LetMeTalk, TouchChat) provide accessible, affordable entry points.
Why It Works
Self-injury is always audible and immediately noticeable. A device that generates speech is equally noticeable. When the device can produce "HELP" or "I HURT" and generate the same immediate response as self-injury, the child has a direct functional substitute. The device competes with self-injury on its own terms.

Critical Rule: The device must be as available as the child's hands. Self-injury is always accessible. Communication must be equally accessible to compete.
Product Options
  • Free AAC apps: LetMeTalk (Android, free), CommunicoTot (free), Cboard (free, web)
  • Paid AAC apps: Avaz (₹2,000–4,000/yr), TouchChat (₹5,000+)
  • Dedicated SGD tablets with protective cases
  • Keyguards for children with motor precision challenges
💰 Price Range: ₹0 (free apps) → ₹2,000–50,000+ (dedicated devices)
🔍Search: "AAC app autism India"

DIY ₹0 Version: Install LetMeTalk or CBoard on any Android device. Program 6 high-priority buttons: HELP · STOP · HURT · WANT · MORE · ALL DONE. Pair with a ₹500 protective case. This is a functional SGD.
Material 3 — Pain and Body Sensation Communication Tools
What It Is
Body maps (front and back body outline), pain scales (Wong-Baker or similar faces-based), and symptom cards for common physical experiences (headache, stomachache, earache, nausea). These tools give children a way to point to pain rather than demonstrate it by hitting the painful location.
Why It Works
Many children hit where it hurts — head-hitting for headaches, stomach-hitting for GI pain. The body map converts this hitting-as-locator into pointing-as-communicator. Same information. No injury.
⚠️ Safety Note
Take ALL pain communications seriously and immediately. A child learning to communicate pain instead of self-injure needs to experience that this communication works. Dismissing pain reports destroys the FCT learning loop.
Product Options
  • Printed body map outlines (A4, laminated) — ₹100–500
  • Wong-Baker pain scale printouts (free: wongbakerfaces.org)
  • Symptom picture cards (downloadable from Teachers Pay Teachers)
  • Body awareness books for children with autism
🔍Search Amazon.in: "body map pain scale children autism"

DIY ₹0 Version: Print a front/back body outline. Create 5-face pain scale from printed emoji faces (😀😐😕😢😫). Print 6–8 common symptom pictures. Laminate. Total cost: ₹30–50.
Material 4 — Emotional Expression Visuals and Regulation Tools
Function Addressed: Emotional state communication — distress, fear, overwhelm, frustration
What It Is
Feeling faces cards at multiple intensities (calm → worried → upset → crisis), Zones of Regulation materials (green/yellow/orange/red), body-emotion connection cards showing body sensations linked to emotional states, and regulation choice boards showing what helps at each zone.
Why It Works
Self-injury often communicates emotional states — "I am overwhelmed and cannot bear this" — that the child has no emotional vocabulary to name. When "I'm in red zone" can be pointed to on a card, the child communicates the same information that the self-injury was communicating, without the harm. Paired with regulation options, the board also suggests solutions.
Product Options — ₹200–1,000
  • Zones of Regulation kit (official or printed)
  • Feelings thermometer posters
  • Emotion faces cards (printed or laminated sets)
  • Body-emotion sensation cards
🔍Search Amazon.in: "emotion faces cards autism zones regulation"

DIY ₹0 Version: Draw 4 stick figures at different upset levels (calm, worried, upset, crisis). Color them green/yellow/orange/red. Paste regulation options next to each. Laminate. Post at child's eye height in 3 rooms.
Material 5 — Request and Rejection Communication Systems
What It Is
"I WANT" sentence strips paired with picture options, "ALL DONE" and "MORE" cards, "YES" and "NO" symbols, and break/stop cards for demands. Gives children exact words for requesting and refusing — the two communicative functions that drive the largest proportion of communication-based SIB.
Why It Works
Self-injury that means "I want X" or "I don't want this" will persist until something else gets X or stops this equally well and equally fast. The design principle is non-negotiable: make communication the easier path. If navigating a complex system takes 30 seconds but hitting takes 1 second, hitting will continue.

Material 6 — Attention / Help-Seeking Alternatives
What It Is
Call buttons or bells that reliably summon adults, "HELP" cards that are always honored, colored flag systems (raise red card = come immediately), and vibrating attention-getters. Any device or symbol that reliably produces adult attention when used — making self-injury unnecessary for obtaining presence or assistance.
Why It Works
For children whose SIB functions as attention-seeking, the only reason hitting works is because it works — every time. Your job is to make the alternative work equally reliably. The call button is not more sophisticated than hitting. But if it works every single time, and is as immediately present as the child's hands, it competes.

DIY ₹0 Version: Make a laminated "HELP" card in red, A6 size. Commit to responding within 10–15 seconds every single time it's presented. Log your response rate. If it's not near 100%, the system is not yet working — adjust your response consistency before upgrading the tool.
Material 7 — Escape and Break Request Systems
What It Is
Break cards (clearly labeled, child-sized, always present during demands), "TOO HARD" signals, "ALL DONE" cards, and timer-based break systems. Gives children a non-harmful way to escape from aversive demands, environments, or sensory situations.
Why It Works
Self-injury that produces escape will continue until something else produces escape equally fast and reliably. Honoring a break card is not "giving in" — it is teaching the child that communication produces results. This is the foundational principle of FCT. Every honored break card is a lesson: "my voice works."
Product Options — ₹100–400
  • Printed BREAK cards (A6, laminated, red border)
  • "Too Hard" task cards
  • Countdown timer visuals (for "break ends in 5 minutes")
  • Break kit box (fidget tools + quiet activity for break time)
🔍Search Amazon.in: "break card autism demand avoidance ABA"

DIY ₹0 Version: Print one A6 card: BREAK (red background, white bold text). Laminate. Keep it attached to the activity area. Every time the child hands it to you — honor it immediately with a defined 3–5 minute break. Success looks like: card use increases → SIB decreases.
Material 8 — Visual Schedules and Predictability Supports
What It Is
Visual schedules showing current activity, what's next, and upcoming preferred events. First-Then boards, Now-Next visuals, transition countdown timers, and "finished" indicators. These materials answer the question that SIB was communicating: What is happening? When does this end? What comes after?
Why It Works
When the visual schedule answers "What's coming?" before the child's anxiety escalates to SIB, the SIB trigger is removed at the source. The information replaces the distress that was generating the behavioral question.

Material 9 — FCT Implementation System
Canon Category: FCT Protocol Materials / ABA Implementation Kits Function Addressed: Systematic, all-functions replacement — the complete intervention framework

FCT implementation materials are the system that ties all 8 previous materials together: individualized replacement communication forms matched to this child's function, FCT teaching protocols, reinforcement delivery systems, data collection forms, prompt hierarchy guides, and partner training materials for all caregivers.

These materials support the systematic, consistent, data-driven implementation that turns 8 individual communication tools into a coordinated replacement program. Before You Begin: The Safety Gate for D-410
🔴 RED — DO NOT PROCEED
  • Child shows signs of medical injury from current SIB (open wounds, dental damage, signs of concussion)
  • No professional functional assessment has been conducted and SIB is severe (daily, high-force, causing injury)
  • SIB has an identified medical cause (GI pain, ear infection, dental pain) that has not been treated
  • Child is currently in a crisis state, actively engaged in SIB, extremely dysregulated
If any RED condition is present: Seek immediate medical or professional consultation. Call Pinnacle Helpline 9100 181 181 for same-day guidance.
🟡 AMBER — MODIFY Before Proceeding
  • Child is slightly dysregulated today — use simplified version (single communication board only, 5-min session)
  • SIB occurred within the last 2 hours — allow full regulation recovery before communication teaching
  • You are a new communication partner — introduce yourself to the system gently
  • Child has a history of multiple SIB functions — confirm primary function before selecting first material
🟢 GREEN — PROCEED When:
  • Child is fed, rested, and in a baseline regulated state
  • At least one communication system is prepared and accessible
  • All caregivers in the environment know to honor the communication attempts
  • A professional (SLP or BCBA) has been consulted or is guiding the plan
  • You have 10–20 uninterrupted minutes available

🔴ABSOLUTE RED LINES — Stop Immediately if: SIB escalates severely during communication teaching | Child shows signs of pain, injury, or medical distress | Child becomes completely dysregulated and the communication system is inaccessible | Communication attempts are being ignored or punished by another caregiver
📞9100 181 181 — Free, 16+ languages, available now 📖Indian Journal of Pediatrics RCT (2019): Home-based intervention safety protocols. DOI:10.1007/s12098-018-2747-4
The Communication-Ready Environment
Setup Checklist — Prepare Your Space Before Every Session
Remove competing stimuli
TV off, siblings elsewhere briefly — quiet focus environment
Communication board/device within arm's reach
Not on the shelf. Not in the bag. Within reach, always.
Break card physically attached to the activity/table surface
Accessible before the need escalates, not after
Call button or help signal physically accessible
Within the child's reach at all times during session
Reinforcers visible and ready
Reward jar, sticker sheet — visible so the child knows what's available
Parent seated at child's level
No looming, no standing above — face-to-face, floor level if needed
Data sheet ready
3-column: Time | Communication Used | SIB y/n
Timer visible
Visual countdown — child knows when the activity ends
Environment Specifications:💡 Warm, natural lighting (not fluorescent) | 🔊 Quiet or gentle background music | 🌡 Comfortable temperature | 📐 Enough space to move away without obstruction 📖PMC10955541 — Meta-analysis: Structured environment + 1:1 sessions showed maximum effectiveness.

Postpone + note reason on data sheet
📖ABA Setting Events: Antecedent manipulation and setting events determine intervention effectiveness. Readiness assessment is a core ABA session protocol component.
STEP 1 of 6
The Invitation — Entering Communication Together
"Hey [child's name]. I see you. We're going to practice using your [board/device/card] together. No pressure. Let's just try."
Body Language Guidance
  • Get to the child's physical level (seated on floor, crouched, face-to-face)
  • Warm, open posture — no crossed arms, no hovering
  • Offer the communication tool with two hands, at their eye level
  • Wait. Do not fill the silence immediately. Give 5–10 seconds for processing.
Timing: 30–60 seconds
✅ Acceptance Cues (what to look for)
  • Child looks at the tool
  • Child reaches toward it
  • Child relaxes slightly (body posture loosens)
  • Child makes eye contact, however brief
⚠️ Resistance Cues and Response
  • Child turns away → Wait 10 seconds, try again once. If still resistant: sit nearby, show the tool casually, reduce demand to zero.
  • Child shows pre-SIB signs → Immediately offer break card. "You can have a break." Honor it.
📖ABA Pairing Procedures: Establishing motivating operations before demand placement. OT "Just-Right Challenge" principle.
STEP 2 of 6
The Engagement — Introducing the Communication Tool
"This is your [HELP card / board / device]. When you need help, you can show me this [point/demonstrate]. I will always listen. Always."
How to Introduce the Material
  • Hold the communication tool at the child's eye level
  • Point to the most critical symbol first (HELP or HURT or ALL DONE — whichever matches their primary SIB function)
  • Demonstrate: "If you press this — [demonstrate] — I will come. I will always come."
  • Model it yourself: press the HELP button, respond to yourself enthusiastically
  • Invite: offer the tool to the child with no demand attached
Response Indicators
✅Engagement: Child examines the tool, presses/touches a symbol ✅Tolerance: Child doesn't reject the tool, maintains proximity ⚠️Avoidance: Child moves away — reduce demand, increase playfulness, try again with lower stakes
Reinforcement Cue
Every time the child touches the communication tool (even incidentally): "Yes! Great touching your board!" Reinforce the approach, not yet the function.
Timing: 1–3 minutes
📖PMC11506176 — Structured material introduction in evidence-based practice for ASD. ABA reinforcement scheduling.
STEP 3 of 6
The Therapeutic Action — Teaching the Replacement Communication
Create a situation where the child's SIB function is naturally activated — their primary need is present. The moment you see pre-SIB signs (tension building, frustration rising, the look in their eyes), prompt the communication tool immediately. Deliver the function the instant they use the tool. The child's brain learns: this communication produces the same result as self-injury.
For Attention/Help-Seeking SIB
  1. Be slightly unavailable (phone in hand, across the room)
  1. See pre-SIB signs
  1. Prompt: physically guide child's hand to HELP card or call button
  1. Child activates signal → YOU RESPOND IMMEDIATELY, enthusiastically
  1. Reinforce: "You used your HELP card! I came! That worked!"
For Escape/Avoidance SIB
  1. Present a mildly non-preferred demand
  1. See pre-SIB signs or resistance
  1. Prompt: guide child to BREAK card
  1. Child hands you BREAK card → STOP the demand immediately
  1. Reinforce: "Break card! Yes! Break time."
For Pain/Distress Communication
  1. During any moment of apparent discomfort
  1. See pre-SIB signs (touching painful area, agitation)
  1. Prompt: guide child's hand to body map
  1. Child points or gestures to location → respond with care and action
  1. Reinforce: "You showed me where it hurts. Thank you. Let me help."

Common Execution Errors:❌ Waiting too long after SIB begins before prompting → Pre-empt at the first sign, not after SIB | ❌ Delayed response after communication → Must be immediate (within 3 seconds) | ❌ Requiring perfect communication form → An approximation counts. A gesture toward the card counts.
Duration: 3–5 minutes of natural opportunity practice 📖PMC10955541 — FCT: Function-matched replacement with immediate reinforcement. PMC1286182 — Original FCT efficacy research.
STEP 4 of 6
Repeat & Vary — Building the Habit
Repetition Guidance
  • Target: 3–8 natural opportunities per session
  • Method: Create or capture natural moments where the SIB function is activated
  • Do not manufacture artificial stress — natural needs are enough
  • Vary the communication partner (parent, grandparent, sibling) — generalization from day 1
"3 clean, function-matched communication replacements that produce the desired result are worth more than 10 rote repetitions. Quality over quantity. Every successful replacement is a neural pathway being built."
Variation Options
Vary the Communication Form (gradually): Start with the simplest form (physical prompt + card). Fade the physical prompt after 3 consistent uses. Progress: full physical prompt → partial prompt → gesture prompt → independent.
Vary the Setting: Kitchen today. Bedroom tomorrow. Living room after that. Generalization across settings is essential for the replacement to fully replace SIB.
Vary the Communication Partner: If only one parent consistently responds, SIB may continue with other partners who don't honor the communication. Train all caregivers.
Satiation Indicators (stop before these appear)
  • Child increasingly uninterested or avoidant
  • Communication quality decreasing (approximations getting weaker)
  • Any pre-SIB signs emerging without communicative function
📖FCT dosage research: 2–3 sessions per week, embedded in daily routines, is the evidence-supported implementation model. Daily natural opportunities supplement formal sessions.
STEP 5 of 6
Reinforce & Celebrate — Making Communication More Powerful Than Self-Injury

The Reinforcement Principle: The replacement communication must be at least as rewarding as self-injury was effective. Timing Rule (non-negotiable):⏱ Within 3 seconds of communication attempt — every time. Late reinforcement tells the brain: "I used the tool and nothing happened for a while." The lesson is lost.
For HELP Card Use
"You showed me HELP! I came! That's exactly right. [Deliver attention/assistance immediately]."
For BREAK Card Use
"BREAK! Yes! Break is yours. [End demand immediately. Give the defined break]."
For PAIN Communication
"You showed me where it hurts. Thank you so much for telling me. [Take pain seriously, act on it]."
🏷 Canon Products — Reinforcement Menu
The Rosette Imprint Reward Jar — ₹589 | amazon.in/d/02C5R9Jn Token drops for each communication replacement attempt. Visual progress visible to child.
1800+ Reward Stickers — ₹364 | amazon.in/d/01wrHJWX Immediate sticker for each communication success. Builds "communication = reward" neural pathway.
Celebrate the Attempt, Not Just the Perfect Response
An approximation — a hand gesture toward the board, a vocalization while touching the device — is a communication attempt. Reinforce it. Require perfection later. Right now, require only direction.
📖ABA reinforcement principles: Immediate, specific reinforcement increases behavior occurrence. PMC1286182 — FCT: Reinforcement of replacement communication as essential component.
STEP 6 of 6
The Cool-Down — Ending Well
No session ends abruptly. The brain needs to transition. An abrupt ending is itself a communication demand the child may not have tools for yet. The cool-down is part of the therapy.
"Two more [practices/activities/minutes]. Then we're all done." Show the visual: 2 fingers. Then 1 finger. Then "ALL DONE" gesture or card.
⏱ "2 more" warning
Visual + verbal — give the child time to prepare for transition
⏱ "Last one"
Acknowledge the near-end explicitly and calmly
🎉 "ALL DONE! You did it."
Celebrate completion — enthusiastic and genuine
🧘 1–2 minutes preferred calm activity
Child's choice from limited options — their earned reward
📦 Material put-away ritual
Child participates if able: "Can you put the board here?"
🚶 Transition cue to next activity
Visual schedule shows what comes next — no ambiguity

If Child Resists Ending: Offer break card (they can have a break from the transition pressure). "Board/device stays here for next time. It will be ready for you." Use First-Then: "First [put away], Then [preferred activity]"
📖NCAEP Evidence-Based Practices Report (2020): Visual supports and transition aids classified as Tier 1 EBP for autism.
Capture the Data — Right Now
60 seconds of data now = months of progress clarity. The data you collect at home is the data your therapist cannot access anywhere else.

TODAY'S DATE: ___________ COMMUNICATION USED (circle all that apply): Comm Board | AAC Device | Body Map | Emotion Visual | Request Card | Help Signal | Break Card | Schedule | FCT Prompt SELF-INJURY (circle): 0 episodes | 1–2 episodes | 3–5 episodes | 5+ episodes COMMUNICATION WAS HONORED BY PARTNER (circle): Always (100%) | Usually (75%) | Sometimes (50%) | Rarely | Never SESSION NOTES (one sentence): _______________________________________________
Communication ↑ + SIB ↓
FCT is working ✅ — stay the course
Communication ↑ + SIB unchanged
Response consistency problem — check the Reinforce step
Communication = 0 + SIB unchanged
Communication tool not accessible or functional — check Materials and Setup cards
📖BACB Guidelines + Cooper, Heron & Heward (Applied Behavior Analysis, 8th Ed.): ABA data collection standards for behavior-analytic intervention.
The Reality Card — Sessions Don't Always Go Perfectly
"Session abandonment is not failure — it's data. Every imperfect session teaches you something about your child's communication needs."
Child ignored the communication tool completely
Why: The tool may not yet have been paired with the function — the child hasn't learned it "works." Fix: Back to Step 3. Engineer 2–3 immediate, obvious demonstrations that the tool produces the desired result. This is normal at this stage.
SIB occurred before I could prompt the communication tool
Why: The communication tool wasn't accessible fast enough, or warning signs were missed. Fix: Attach the tool to the child's body or the activity surface. Review pre-SIB warning signs for your child. Aim to prompt at the first sign, not after escalation.
Child used the board but I didn't respond immediately
Why: Human — this happens. But it damages the learning loop. Fix: Acknowledge it: "I missed your communication. I'm sorry. Show me again — I'm ready now." For the next week: respond to the tool with priority over any other task.
Child started using the communication tool to get out of everything
Why: Great news — the replacement is working. Now calibrate. Fix: You can increase tolerance gradually but only after the replacement is well-established. Do not deny break cards in the early stage.
One parent honors the system, the other doesn't
Why: Partner inconsistency. Common. Dangerous. Fix: Have the non-implementing partner watch the session. Show them the data. The data is the argument.
Child became severely distressed during the session
Why: Demand may have been above the "just-right challenge" level, or SIB function was misidentified. Fix: Stop. Offer break card. Comfort. Do not re-introduce demands for 20+ minutes. Consult with therapist before next session. 📞9100 181 181
The SIB hasn't decreased at all after 2 weeks
Why: FCT takes 4–12 weeks for primary replacement. 2 weeks is very early. OR: function may be misidentified. OR: response consistency below 80%. Fix: Check response consistency data. If above 80% for 2 weeks with no change: consider functional reassessment.
No Two Children's Communication Needs Are Identical — Adapt & Personalize
🔵 Non-Speaking (0–20 words)
Start at level 2. Single symbol, single function. HELP card only, for 2 weeks, before adding any second function. Less is more. Let the first communication succeed before complicating the system.
🟢 Minimally Verbal (20–100 words)
Combine words with symbols. "Help" word + HELP card together. Reinforce both. The symbol scaffolds the word.
🟡 Motor Challenges
Keyguards, large symbols (A4 vs A6), switch-access AAC, mounting systems. Consult OT for motor access assessment before selecting tools.
🔴 High-Force SIB
Safety equipment first (helmet, wrist guards as temporary protective measures). Parallel FCT simultaneously — protective measures reduce injury while replacement builds. Do NOT use protective measures without building the communication alternative simultaneously.
Age Modifications
  • 2–4 years: Single-symbol, maximum immediacy, maximum reinforcement intensity
  • 5–8 years: Sentence-level, add social functions beyond just needs
  • 9–12 years: Self-monitoring components, peer communication contexts, literacy-based supports if appropriate
📖Individualized intervention planning: Core principle across OT (sensory profile), ABA (function-based), SLP (communication profile) disciplines. Clinical practice guidelines.
Weeks 1–2: Building the Foundation
Foundation Phase — 15% Progress
What "Progress" Actually Looks Like at This Stage
You Will See
You Will NOT See Yet
Child looks at or approaches communication tool
Spontaneous independent use of the tool
Child accepts prompts to use tool without major resistance
Reduction in SIB frequency
1–2 instances of unprompted tool use (may feel accidental)
Consistent communication across all contexts
Caregiver response consistency improving
Generalization to new partners
Parent Emotional Preparation
Week 1–2 is the hardest. The system is new. SIB may briefly increase — this is called an "extinction burst" in behavior science. It means the child is testing whether the new communication works as well as the old. This is a sign the child has understood something is changing. Stay consistent. Do not abandon at this phase.
"If your child attempts the communication tool once today — just once — that is a word replacing a wound. That is progress."
📖PMC11506176 — Intervention outcomes emerge across 6–12 week timelines. Early phase: tolerance and participation markers.
Weeks 3–4: The Neural Pathways Are Forming
Consolidation Phase — 40% Progress
✅ Anticipation Emerging
Child begins to reach for or look at communication tool before the need escalates to SIB
✅ Preference Emergence
Child shows preference for the communication tool over SIB in familiar contexts (though not yet all contexts)
✅ Partner Generalization Beginning
Tool used with at least 2 caregivers, not just the primary implementing parent
✅ SIB Frequency Measurably Declining
Compare weekly totals from your data sheet — the trend should be downward in trained contexts
✅ Communication Quality Improving
Less prompting needed, clearer symbol selection, more deliberate communication attempts

Neural Pathway Formation: What you are witnessing at weeks 3–4 is synaptic strengthening. The pathway "communication tool → desired result" is being reinforced through repetition and consistent outcome. The neural competition between "SIB route" and "communication route" is tilting toward communication. This is biology responding to consistent behavioral practice.
"You may notice that you're more confident too. You can read the pre-SIB signs. You know the prompt sequence. You have data. You are no longer guessing — you are implementing a system."
📖Neuroplasticity: Synaptic strengthening through repeated structured input follows predictable timelines in pediatric populations.
Weeks 5–8: Mastery Indicators
🏆 Mastery Phase — 75% Progress
3+
Contexts for Independent Use
Child uses communication replacement independently with no prompt needed in ≥3 different contexts
50%+
SIB Reduction from Baseline
SIB frequency reduced by ≥50% from baseline per your data sheet
3+
Communication Partners
Communication generalized to ≥3 different communication partners across environments
Generalization Indicators: Tool use appearing in contexts not specifically trained (playground, grandparent's house, school) | Child correcting their own SIB attempt (starting to SIB, stopping, shifting to communication tool) | Novel communication attempts: using the tool for new messages beyond the original 2–3 targets
"Mastery is not the end. It is the evidence that your child's brain has learned that communication works. Now we build the vocabulary — the full language they deserve."
📖PMC10955541 — FCT mastery criteria. BACB behavioral measurement standards. FCT generalization planning.
⚠️ Even in the Celebration Zone — Know When to Pause
🔴 SIB escalating in force or new locations
New forms of SIB appearing, or existing SIB becoming more intense, despite consistent FCT implementation for 4+ weeks → professional functional reassessment needed
🔴 No SIB reduction after 6+ weeks
Suggests function may be misidentified, response consistency may be low, or co-occurring automatic/sensory function not addressed → BCBA consultation urgently
🔴 Communication tool being abandoned by child
After prior use, child stops using the tool and SIB increases → possible extinction burst, possible partner inconsistency, possible function change → review all response data
🔴 New injury or skin damage appearing
Any self-injury causing open wounds, bruising, dental damage, or eye injury → immediate medical evaluation + Pinnacle helpline
🔴 Signs of medical pain emerging
Increased SIB localized to one body area, especially after eating, sleep changes, visible discomfort → rule out medical cause before continuing behavioral intervention
📞Pinnacle Helpline: 9100 181 181 (Free, 24×7, 16+ languages) 📖WHO NCF: Primary health care as platform for early identification. Pinnacle clinical escalation protocols.
From the Field — Families Who Have Walked This Path
Arjun, 5 years — Before
Non-speaking. Hitting his head against walls 20–35 times per day, primarily in demand contexts and when appearing to be in pain. Mother had tried consequence-based approaches for 6 months with no change. No communication system in place.
After 7 weeks (FCT + core communication board + pain body map)
Head-hitting reduced to 3–5 per day, exclusively during novel or extremely aversive situations. Arjun points to his body map for pain communication 8–12 times per day. Requests breaks using a BREAK card independently.
"The first time he pointed to his stomach on the body map instead of hitting his tummy, I stood there crying. He was telling me. He'd always been trying to tell me."
Therapist's Notes: "Arjun had a clear communicative function for all SIB — escape from demands and pain expression. The key was the pain communication board — he used it within 48 hours of introduction."
Meera, 4 years — Before
Minimal verbal. SIB in the form of hand-biting (leaving marks) whenever she wanted something and couldn't request it. Parents had no awareness that communication function was driving the behavior. Had been described by a previous professional as "attention-seeking manipulation."
After 10 weeks (AAC app + request system)
Hand-biting reduced by 85%. Meera has 23 programmed buttons on her AAC app and uses 8–10 spontaneously per day. She can request food, play, and preferred activities.
"We wasted a year trying to 'extinguish' the behavior. The moment we gave her the app, she stopped biting within two weeks. She had things to say. She just needed a way to say them."
Note: Individual results vary. Outcomes depend on function identification, implementation fidelity, and consistency. Questions Parents Ask Most — Answered by the Consortium
"My child has never used any communication tool. Where do I even start?"
Start with one card: HELP or ALL DONE — whichever matches your child's primary SIB function. A single symbol, always present, always honored. Before adding anything else. One symbol working perfectly is worth more than nine symbols working inconsistently.
"Is this the same as PECS? We tried PECS and it didn't work."
FCT uses PECS principles (picture exchange) but the critical difference is function matching. PECS teaches requesting — which is one of four functions SIB can serve. If your child's SIB functions as escape or pain expression, PECS alone won't address it. D-410 covers all four communicative functions.
"We've been told our child's SIB is 'attention-seeking' and to ignore it. Why are you saying the opposite?"
Ignoring communication-function SIB without providing an alternative silences the child without giving them another voice. Research consistently shows that extinction without an alternative communication replacement leads to escalation, not resolution. FCT replaces; extinction alone suppresses.
"How do we know if the SIB is communication-function or sensory-function?"
Key indicators: Does SIB occur in social contexts where someone is present? Does the child look at the caregiver during or after SIB? Does SIB stop when the apparent need is met? If yes to all: communication function is likely primary. See D-411 for sensory-function SIB, which often co-occurs.
"My child's SIB is severe and I'm scared to try this at home without professional help."
You are right to be cautious. Severe SIB warrants professional functional assessment before home implementation. Call 9100 181 181 for immediate professional navigation. Teleconsultation with a BCBA is available within 48 hours.
"The AAC device is too expensive. Can a cheaper option really work?"
Yes. Free apps on existing devices (LetMeTalk on Android) are clinically equivalent to dedicated devices in Phase 1 FCT for most children. The function — giving the child a voice that gets a response — is achievable with ₹0 investment.
"How long before we see results?"
Measurable SIB reduction typically appears in weeks 3–6 of consistent implementation. Some families see early signs within 1–2 weeks. The critical variable is response consistency — not the quality of the tools, but how reliably all caregivers honor the communication attempts.
"What if my child has multiple SIB functions — not just communication?"
Very common. Start with the dominant function (the one that accounts for the most SIB episodes). Once the primary function is addressed and SIB reduces, residual SIB can reveal secondary functions (often sensory — see D-411). Layer the interventions sequentially.
